control_ladder.note_beginner: The larvae live down in the mix, so what you want is a top layer that is not permanently drenched. Instead of pouring over the crop, stand the tray in a shallow bath of water and let the mix pull it up from below, which leaves the top free to dry between rounds. Keeping a little air moving across the tray helps too. Cilantro's 3 to 4 week grow gives gnats a longer run at that damp layer than a quick crop would.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Once the stand has greened, let the top dry back between waterings and feed the tray from below, with air moving over it; larvae depend on medium that stays wet. Over a 3 to 4 week cilantro cycle that wet surface stays on offer far longer than it does on a fast brassica, so the moisture discipline is carrying more of the load here.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Wash and sanitize your trays and start each batch with fresh mix. That is what stops gnats carrying over from one batch to the next, and the payoff is bigger on cilantro, where a single tray sits in the same spot for weeks.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Between batches, sanitizing the trays and going to fresh medium is the step that actually breaks the breeding cycle, and a long cilantro run leans on it harder than a fast brassica turned over quickly does.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Yellow sticky cards, small glue-coated cards that flying insects land on and stick to, will pick up adult gnats if you stand them low, down near the mix. Their main value is the warning: on a crop that occupies the tray for 3 to 4 weeks, noticing numbers while they are still climbing leaves you room to tighten up the watering.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Placed low against the medium, the cards take adults out of the air and, more usefully, register a rising population before it is obvious in the stand. On a 3 to 4 week cilantro run that early read is worth more than on a tray that turns over quickly, since the numbers have room to compound first.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Do not sow the seed too thickly. A crowded stand traps damp, still air right down at the soil line, which is where the rot starts, and on cilantro that stand is standing there for 3 to 4 weeks.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hold the seeding rate down. A dense stand keeps a humid, stagnant layer sitting at the soil line, and cilantro keeps that layer standing for weeks where a quicker crop would already have been cut.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the mix just damp, about as wet as a wrung-out sponge, rather than soggy. Once the leaves are up, water from the bottom by setting the tray in shallow water, so the surface itself stays drier.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Wrung-sponge moisture, then bottom-watering once the crop has greened, keeps the surface off the wet end of the range these fungi need.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep a small fan running so gentle air is moving across the tray the whole time. Cilantro asks for that more than a fast crop does: between the blackout, the covered dark stretch at the start, and a grow that runs 3 to 4 weeks, the little canopy of leaves stays damp and crowded for a long stretch.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Constant gentle airflow across the tray. A long blackout followed by a 3 to 4 week grow holds a humid, crowded canopy over the medium far longer than a quick crop does, so moving air is carrying more of the prevention on this crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: There is no spray that belongs on greens you cut and eat raw, so prevention has to carry this one on its own. Wash your trays and sanitize them between batches. A tray that has gone heavily moldy is better composted than rescued, so start that batch over in clean trays.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A raw cut crop has nothing to rescue it, which puts the weight on sanitation: trays sanitized between cycles, and a badly affected tray composted and restarted clean rather than nursed along.
